You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Morgan Stanley CPO GlassBridge Deep Update: GlassBridge Replacement Anxiety, TSMC 25kwpm PIC and FAU Supply Chain Repricing

TEXT:
TLDR
1. GlassBridge first changes long-term expectations. It integrates glass waveguides, pluggable connections, and passive alignment into a unified interface solution to address high channel counts, testability, repairability, and reflow compatibility issues. However, it is currently closer to edge coupling and linear optical fiber layouts, making it difficult in the short term to directly replace TSMC COUPE, Nvidia, AMD, and Ayar Labs, who are still advancing the grating coupling main path.
2. The CPO mass production gatekeeper is TSMC PIC. Morgan Stanley expects TSMC PIC capacity to increase from the current approximately 500 wafers/month to 10kwpm in Q2 2026, 15kwpm in Q4 2026, and at least 25kwpm in 2028. If downstream assembly yield improves from 20% to 50%, actual optical engine shipments could move from millions to tens of millions.
3. Test efficiency is the hidden bottleneck. Insertion 2 testing after SoIC has already improved from one wafer per day (H2 2025) to one wafer every 6 hours (UTC+8); the next 6-12 months aim for one wafer every 3-4 hours (UTC+8). This pace will determine the sloping order trend for equipment and fixture companies such as Chroma, FormFactor/Wi, Keystone Technology, and Honjin as CPO transitions from samples and NRE to MP.
4. FAU supply chain still has a two-year window. Morgan Stanley judges that in 2026 Nvidia Spectrum CPO switches will be the primary mass production revenue driver for FOCI, with FOCI holding about 40% share in Nvidia CPO FAU. Nvidia's contribution to FOCI's revenue could rise from 18% (2026) to 80% (2028). GlassBridge may suppress the upper end of the valuation band but acts as a more distant risk factor in the short term.
5. AllRing’s realized quality leans closer to advanced packaging. AllRing’s CoWoS business remains its foundation, with CPO equipment revenue expected to rise from 11% (2026) to 26% (2028), and CPO equipment gross margin can reach 55-60%. These companies profit from packaging expansion, optical engine coupling, and AOI certainty, not relying solely on a single optical route.
6. Investment ranking enters phase 2. Phase 1 was buying CPO concept and optical module beta; phase 2 will prioritize mass production gates: first TSMC PIC capacity expansion, Insertion testing, Spectrum/Quantum/Rubin Ultra nodes, then see if FOCI, Tianfu Communication, AllRing, FormFactor/Wi, Keystone Technology, and other suppliers turn shares into revenue and profit.
Table of Contents Join Knowledge Planet to view the complete original report and reference research reports in full text

2. In the short term, the main path remains in TSMC COUPE and grating coupling
3. TSMC PIC capacity determines the upper limit of CPO shipments
4. Insertion testing is an underestimated mass production gate
5. Supply chain order: FAU realize first, GlassBridge suppresses the long-term
6. FOCI: transition in 2026, begin tracking revenue slope in 2027

This CPO update brings optical module trading back to mass production details: GlassBridge brings long-term replacement pressure; in 2026-27 attention should instead be paid to TSMC PIC capacity, post-SoIC test efficiency, realization of FAU/equipment supply chain revenues, and when GlassBridge transitions from sample to customer standard interface.
1. GlassBridge pushes the CPO debate to the packaging interface layer
The most valuable part of this report is moving the CPO discussion from “Will optical modules be replaced?” to “How will optics connect to silicon photonic chips?” Over the past year, the market has become more familiar with terms like 800G, 1.6T, 3.2T, LPO, CPO, NPO at the system level, but true production bottlenecks often come from finer details: how optical fiber arrays are fixed, PIC testing, how optical engines connect to switch chips, packaging, board-level interconnects, and whether repairs are possible if faults occur.
GlassBridge’s emergence makes this issue even more acute. Traditional FAUs place fibers in a V-Groove, passively aligned to the PIC via glass/silicon/quartz substrates. The advantage is its maturity, low loss, and customization; however, as channel count and density increase, assembly, alignment and consistency become more difficult. GlassBridge instead packages glass waveguides, connectors, and passive alignment into a bridge-type structure aiming to improve manufacturability and maintainability for high-density optical access.
[...]
This is not a simple “new scheme replaces old.” GlassBridge is more about evolving the interface from a one-time assembly into a systemic connection architecture: allowing testing first and then connection, also making repair and platformization easier. However, CPO’s largest commercial issue is still ramping mass production, not concept advancement. In the short term, trades should focus not only on whose technical route sounds better, but who actually enters real customer nodes such as TSMC COUPE, Nvidia Spectrum/Quantum, AMD MI500, Ayar Labs.
[...]
The more realistic near-term mainline is TSMC COUPE. The report asserts TSMC COUPE and the paths of Nvidia, AMD, and Ayar Labs are more likely to continue with grating coupling in the next few years because it’s easier to enter near-term mass production. GlassBridge is currently more like a high-density bridge solution within edge coupling, solving some interface pain points first before its potential expansion into more system architectures.
[...]
Under this framework, CPO trading should upgrade from “Will optical modules be replaced by CPO?” to “Which nodes will get orders first?” The first step is Nvidia Spectrum CPO switch and Broadcom Tomahawk-type scale-out switching; step two is AMD MI500, Ayar Labs, AWS Trainium, etc. at the scale-up or chiplet/OIO node; step three is future Feynman Ultra, Rubin Ultra, and even higher density connection schemes. GlassBridge offers more imagination at the third step, but for the first two requires further validation in real customer roadmaps.
[...]
The CPO switch shipment curve also supports this. The report projects 23k units in 2026, mainly 100T, with Nvidia Spectrum dominating; 59k by 2027, and about 200k by 2030. The curve is not linear; inflection points depend on system introductions of Spectrum, Quantum, Tomahawk, Rubin Ultra, MI500/MI600, as well as cloud vendors’ self-developed ASICs. Suppliers who only secure NRE and small-batch samples will find it hard to support high valuations; those onboarded to the mainstream platform MP will see valuation models shift significantly.
[...]
The FAU supply chain still has a two-year window. The report explicitly mentions that FOCI’s CPO MP revenue will start from July 2026 and ramp in 2027, with early share mainly from Spectrum CPO switches. Tianfu Communication, FOCI, Senko are at Nvidia’s 2026 scale-out CPO as the main FAU supplier group. For FAU companies, GlassBridge is a valuation ceiling, not a 2026 revenue collapse indicator.
[...]
The report’s main assumption: 2026 mainstream scale-out CPO optical engine production at 600,000–1 million units, about 20,000 CPO switches. Tianfu Communication, FOCI, and Senko are the major FAU suppliers, with FOCI at about 40% share. Nvidia’s contribution to FOCI revenue is expected to grow from 18% in 2026 to 42% in 2027 and 80% by 2028. This curve means FOCI’s investment thesis is not about 2026 profit, but 2027 customer ramp, and 2028 customer diversification.
[...]
FOCI’s strengths are clear customer and product lines. Nvidia scale-out leads with Spectrum/Quantum; future scale-up includes OIO/Feynman Ultra; AMD MI500/MI600, Ayar Labs, AWS Trainium, Marvell Technology, MediaTek are all mid-to-long term customer leads. The report notes FOCI already has more than 10 customer prototype projects contributing NRE in 2026, entering mass production in 2027-28—these are not fully modeled and can form the “bull case.”
